       local = knitr::knit_global())

## Overview

This report investigates associations among body mass index (BMI),
self-reported high blood pressure, age, income, and diabetes status
using the 2015 BRFSS Diabetes Health Indicators dataset.

The analysis combines descriptive statistics, confidence intervals,
hypothesis testing, analysis of variance (ANOVA), and multiple
linear regression.

The findings are observational and should not be interpreted
as evidence of causation or as clinically validated risk estimates.

## Dataset

The analysis uses 253,680 survey records with 21 health and
demographic indicators and one diabetes-status outcome.

The statistical results use conventional unweighted methods
and do not account for the complex BRFSS survey design.



## High Blood Pressure Distribution

We first examine the prevalence of self-reported high blood pressure
among the 253,680 survey respondents.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-high-bp
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Distribution of Self-Reported High Blood Pressure"

knitr::kable(
  bp_summary,
  col.names = c("Blood Pressure Status", "Respondents", "Share (%)"),
  format = "html"
)
```

Approximately 42.9% of respondents reported having high blood
pressure, compared with 57.1% who did not.



### High Blood Pressure Visualization

```{r}
#| label: fig-high-bp
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of self-reported high blood pressure among BRFSS respondents."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center

bp_bars <- barplot(
  bp_counts,
  col = c("#A8BED0", "#2E6487"),
  border = NA,
  ylim = c(0, max(bp_counts) * 1.15),
  main = "Self-Reported High Blood Pressure",
  xlab = "High Blood Pressure Status",
  ylab = "Number of Respondents"
)

text(
  x = bp_bars,
  y = as.numeric(bp_counts),
  labels = paste0(
    format(as.integer(bp_counts), big.mark = ","),
    " (", bp_percent, "%)"
  ),
  pos = 3,
  cex = 0.9
)
```


## Body Mass Index (BMI) Analysis

Body Mass Index (BMI) is a quantitative health indicator
included in the BRFSS dataset. We examine its distribution
and descriptive statistics to understand the characteristics
of the surveyed population.

### Descriptive Statistics

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bmi-summary
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive Statistics for BMI"

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Statistic = names(bmi_stats),
    Value = round(as.numeric(bmi_stats), 2)
  ),
  col.names = c("Statistic", "Value"),
  format = "html"
)
```

The average BMI among the 253,680 respondents was **28.38**,
with a median of **27** and a standard deviation of **6.61**.
Observed BMI values ranged from **12 to 98**.

### BMI Distribution

```{r}
#| label: fig-bmi-distribution
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of BMI across BRFSS respondents."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center

hist(
  data$BMI,
  breaks = 30,
  col = "#A8BED0",
  border = "white",
  main = "Distribution of Body Mass Index",
  xlab = "BMI",
  ylab = "Number of Respondents"
)
```

The distribution is right-skewed, with most BMI values
concentrated toward the lower end of the observed range
and a smaller number of respondents reporting substantially
higher BMI values.



## BMI by High Blood Pressure Status

To explore the relationship between BMI and high blood pressure,
we compare BMI distributions among respondents who reported
high blood pressure and those who did not.

### Group Comparison

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bmi-by-bp
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "BMI Summary by High Blood Pressure Status"

knitr::kable(
  bmi_by_bp,
  col.names = c(
    "Blood Pressure Status",
    "Respondents",
    "Mean BMI",
    "Median BMI",
    "Standard Deviation"
  ),
  format = "html",
  big.mark = ","
)
```

Respondents reporting high blood pressure had a higher average
BMI (**30.01**) compared with those without high blood
pressure (**27.16**).

This represents a difference of approximately **2.85 BMI points**.

### Distribution Comparison

```{r}
#| label: fig-bmi-by-bp
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "BMI distributions by self-reported high blood pressure status. Outlier points are hidden for readability."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center

boxplot(
  BMI ~ factor(HighBP,
               levels = c(0, 1),
               labels = c("No high BP", "High BP")),
  data = data,
  col = c("#A8BED0", "#2E6487"),
  border = "#334155",
  outline = FALSE,
  main = "BMI by High Blood Pressure Status",
  xlab = "High Blood Pressure Status",
  ylab = "BMI"
)
```

### Interpretation

The boxplot illustrates differences in the central tendency
and variability of BMI between the two groups.

Respondents with high blood pressure generally had higher
BMI values than those without high blood pressure.

These findings establish a **descriptive association**,
not a causal relationship between BMI and high blood pressure.



## Confidence Interval Analysis

Confidence intervals provide a range of plausible values
for a population mean, based on sample observations and
statistical assumptions.

We constructed conventional 95% confidence intervals for
overall mean BMI and for two age groups: respondents aged
18–24 and respondents aged 50–54.

### Overall and Age-Group Confidence Intervals

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bmi-confidence-intervals
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "95% Confidence Intervals for Mean BMI"

ci_summary <- data.frame(
  Group = c(
    "All respondents",
    "Ages 18–24",
    "Ages 50–54"
  ),
  Respondents = format(
    c(n, n1, n2),
    big.mark = ",",
    scientific = FALSE,
    trim = TRUE
  ),
  Mean_BMI = round(
    c(mean_bmi, xbar1, xbar2),
    2
  ),
  CI_95 = c(
    sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci95_bmi[1], ci95_bmi[2]),
    sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci95_1[1], ci95_1[2]),
    sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci95_2[1], ci95_2[2])
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  ci_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Population Group",
    "Respondents",
    "Mean BMI",
    "95% Confidence Interval"
  ),
  format = "html",
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "c")
)
```

### Interpretation

**Overall BMI.** The sample mean BMI was 28.38, with a
conventional 95% confidence interval of [28.36, 28.41].
The narrow interval reflects the large sample size.

**Age-group comparison.** Respondents aged 18–24 had a
mean BMI of 26.09, compared with 28.94 among respondents
aged 50–54.

The corresponding confidence intervals do not overlap,
and the observed difference in mean BMI is approximately
2.85 points.

The younger age group has a wider confidence interval,
consistent with its smaller sample size.

### Statistical Considerations

These intervals use standard unweighted methods that
assume independent observations. They do not account for
the BRFSS complex survey sampling design.

Consequently, they should not be interpreted as
survey-design-adjusted estimates for the U.S. population.



## Hypothesis Testing

We conducted two hypothesis tests to investigate BMI in the
surveyed population and its association with reported
diabetes status.

### Statistical Test Results

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hypothesis-tests
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of BMI Hypothesis Tests"

# Reuse the exact tests performed in the R script
one_sample_test <- t.test(
  data$BMI,
  mu = 25,
  alternative = "greater"
)

two_sample_test <- t.test(
  no_diabetes,
  diabetes
)

test_summary <- data.frame(
  Test = c(
    "One-sample t-test",
    "Welch two-sample t-test"
  ),
  Comparison = c(
    "Mean BMI > 25",
    "No diabetes vs. diabetes"
  ),
  T_Statistic = round(c(
    one_sample_test$statistic,
    two_sample_test$statistic
  ), 2),
  Degrees_Freedom = round(c(
    one_sample_test$parameter,
    two_sample_test$parameter
  ), 1),
  P_Value = c(
    "< 0.001",
    "< 0.001"
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  test_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Test",
    "Comparison",
    "t-statistic",
    "Degrees of Freedom",
    "p-value"
  ),
  format = "html"
)
```

### One-Sample t-Test: Mean BMI Greater Than 25

**Research question:** Is the average BMI greater than 25?

- **Null hypothesis:** Population mean BMI is at most 25.
- **Alternative hypothesis:** Population mean BMI exceeds 25.
- **Sample mean BMI:** 28.38

The one-sample t-test produced a t-statistic of approximately
257.78 (p < 0.001).

We reject the null hypothesis under the conventional test
assumptions. The observed mean BMI exceeds the benchmark by
approximately **3.38 BMI points**.

The large sample size contributes to the very high test
statistic and small p-value.

### Welch Two-Sample t-Test: Diabetes Status

**Research question:** Does mean BMI differ between respondents
reporting diabetes and those reporting no diabetes?

- **Null hypothesis:** The two groups have equal population mean BMI.
- **Alternative hypothesis:** Their population mean BMIs differ.

| Reported diabetes status | Mean BMI |
|---|---:|
| No diabetes | 27.74 |
| Diabetes | 31.94 |

The Welch two-sample t-test produced a t-statistic of
approximately -101.38 (p < 0.001).

Respondents reporting diabetes had a mean BMI approximately
**4.20 points higher** than respondents reporting no diabetes.

Respondents reporting prediabetes were excluded from this
two-group comparison.

### Interpretation

Both tests show statistically significant results under
conventional unweighted assumptions. However, these tests
do not account for the BRFSS complex survey sampling design.

The findings describe differences and associations in
reported health indicators; they do not establish causation.



## BMI Differences Across Age Groups

To investigate how BMI varies across age categories, we compared
mean BMI across the 13 age groups represented in the BRFSS dataset.

The original age categories were preserved rather than replacing
them with artificially generated exact ages.

### Mean BMI by Age Group

```{r}
#| label: fig-bmi-age-groups
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Mean BMI across the 13 BRFSS age categories."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center

plot(
  age_bmi_summary$Age,
  age_bmi_summary$BMI,
  type = "b",
  pch = 19,
  main = "Mean BMI by Age Group",
  xlab = "Age Group (1 = 18-24, 13 = 80+)",
  ylab = "Mean BMI"
)
```

Mean BMI generally increases from early adulthood through
middle age, peaking around ages 45–49, before declining
among older age groups.

This is a cross-sectional comparison of respondents, not
evidence of how an individual's BMI changes over time.

### One-Way ANOVA

We conducted a one-way analysis of variance to determine
whether mean BMI differs across age groups.

**Null hypothesis:** All 13 age groups have equal population
mean BMI.

**Alternative hypothesis:** At least one age group has a
different population mean BMI.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-anova
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "One-Way ANOVA: BMI by Age Group"

knitr::kable(
  as.data.frame(anova_table),
  digits = 3,
  format = "html",
  col.names = c(
    "Degrees of Freedom",
    "Sum of Squares",
    "Mean Square",
    "F-statistic",
    "p-value"
  )
)
```

### Effect Size and Interpretation

```{r}
#| label: tbl-anova-effect
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "ANOVA Results and Effect Size"

anova_results <- data.frame(
  Metric = c(
    "F-statistic",
    "Between-group degrees of freedom",
    "Residual degrees of freedom",
    "p-value",
    "Eta-squared",
    "Variance explained"
  ),
  Value = c(
    round(anova_table$`F value`[1], 1),
    as.character(anova_table$Df[1]),
    as.character(anova_table$Df[2]),
    "< 0.001",
    round(eta_squared, 4),
    paste0(round(eta_squared * 100, 2), "%")
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  anova_results,
  format = "html"
)
```

The ANOVA identified statistically significant differences
in mean BMI across age groups:

**F(12, 253667) = 332.1, p < 0.001.**

However, statistical significance does not necessarily
indicate a large association.

The eta-squared effect size was approximately **0.0155**,
meaning age-group membership explained only **1.55% of the
observed variation in BMI**.

These findings indicate meaningful descriptive differences
across age categories, but substantial BMI variation remains
unexplained by age group alone.

As with the other analyses, the conventional ANOVA does not
account for the complex BRFSS survey sampling design.



## Multiple Linear Regression

We fitted a multiple linear regression model to examine
how BMI varies across age and income categories.

Both predictors use their original BRFSS categorical
values rather than artificially generated exact ages
or income amounts.

The model is specified as:

\[
BMI = \beta_0 + \text{Age Group Effects}
+ \text{Income Group Effects} + \varepsilon
\]

### Model Performance

```{r}
#| label: tbl-regression-fit
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Multiple Linear Regression Model Summary"

reg_summary <- summary(bmi_group_model)
f_stat <- reg_summary$fstatistic

model_fit <- data.frame(
  Metric = c(
    "Observations",
    "R-squared",
    "Adjusted R-squared",
    "Residual standard error",
    "F-statistic",
    "Model p-value"
  ),
  Value = c(
    format(nobs(bmi_group_model), big.mark = ","),
    sprintf("%.4f", reg_summary$r.squared),
    sprintf("%.4f", reg_summary$adj.r.squared),
    sprintf("%.3f", reg_summary$sigma),
    sprintf(
      "F(%d, %d) = %.1f",
      f_stat[2], f_stat[3], f_stat[1]
    ),
    "< 0.001"
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  model_fit,
  col.names = c("Metric", "Value"),
  format = "html"
)
```

The model is statistically significant overall
(F(19, 253660) = 456.6, p < 0.001).

However, its **R-squared of 0.0331** indicates that age
and income categories collectively explain only
approximately **3.31% of the observed variation in BMI**.

This is relatively low explanatory power, suggesting
that most BMI variation is associated with factors
outside this model.

### Regression Coefficients

The reference categories are:

- **Age Group 1:** 18–24 years
- **Income Group 1:** Less than $10,000

Each age-group coefficient represents the estimated
difference in BMI relative to ages 18–24, holding
income category constant.

Each income-group coefficient represents the estimated
difference relative to the lowest income category,
holding age group constant.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-regression-coefficients
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Regression Coefficients and 95% Confidence Intervals"

coef_matrix <- reg_summary$coefficients
ci_matrix <- confint(bmi_group_model, level = 0.95)

coef_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = rownames(coef_matrix),
  Estimate = round(coef_matrix[, 1], 3),
  CI_Lower = round(ci_matrix[, 1], 3),
  CI_Upper = round(ci_matrix[, 2], 3),
  P_Value = ifelse(
    coef_matrix[, 4] < 0.001,
    "< 0.001",
    sprintf("%.3f", coef_matrix[, 4])
  ),
  row.names = NULL
)

knitr::kable(
  coef_table,
  col.names = c(
    "Predictor",
    "Estimate",
    "95% CI Lower",
    "95% CI Upper",
    "p-value"
  ),
  format = "html"
)
```

### Key Findings

**Age differences.** Respondents aged 45–49
(Age Group 6) had an estimated BMI approximately
**3.44 points higher** than respondents aged 18–24,
holding income category constant.

**Income differences.** Respondents in the highest
income category ($75,000 or more) had an estimated
BMI approximately **2.40 points lower** than those
in the lowest income category, holding age group
constant.

**Older age groups.** Age Group 13 (80+) was not
statistically significantly different from
Age Group 1 after adjusting for income
(p = 0.191).

### Interpretation and Limitations

Although the regression is statistically significant,
its explanatory power is limited.

Age and income categories capture only a small
portion of BMI variation in this dataset.

The results describe statistical associations,
not causal effects.
